records.topic: What If the Moon Kept Drifting Away?
records.hook: Why the Moon drifts 38 millimetres farther every year.
records.openingLine: Why the Moon drifts 38 millimetres farther every year.
records.secondBeat: That's about as fast as your fingernails grow.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal interaction transfers Earth's spin energy to the Moon, slowly raising its orbit
records.scenarioChange: the Moon kept receding for hundreds of millions of years
records.expectedConsequence: a smaller-looking Moon, and eventually no total solar eclipses
records.coreQuestion: If the Moon kept drifting away, what would we lose first?
records.misconception: The Moon isn't fixed in place; it recedes by centimetres every year.
visualScenes: laser beam hitting a lunar reflector
angular size comparison Moon versus Sun
editorialTitles: Why the Moon Is Slowly Leaving Us
What Happens When Eclipses End

facts.claim: Measurements from laser reflectors left during the Apollo missions have found that the Moon's distance increases by 38 mm (1.5 in) per year, roughly the rate at which human fingernails grow.
It orbits Earth at an average distance of 384,399 kilometers (238,854 mi).
On average the Moon's angular diameter is about 0.52°, roughly the same apparent size as the Sun.
As the Moon's orbit around Earth is inclined by about 5.145° to the orbit of Earth around the Sun, eclipses do not occur at every full and new moon.

narration.text: Why the Moon drifts 38 millimetres farther every year.
That's about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Apollo's laser reflectors let us measure it.
It orbits about 384,399 kilometres away today.
From Earth, it spans about 0.52 degrees, like the Sun.
As it recedes, it will look smaller than the Sun.
Then total solar eclipses will stop happening.
So perfect eclipses are a temporary coincidence.

records.topic: What If You Lived on Mercury?
records.hook: Why one Mercury day lasts 176 Earth days.
records.openingLine: Why one Mercury day lasts 176 Earth days.
records.secondBeat: That's twice as long as its 88-day year.
records.scientificMechanism: a slow 3:2 spin–orbit resonance and no atmosphere create extreme day–night temperature swings
records.scenarioChange: someone tried to live on Mercury
records.expectedConsequence: months-long days reaching about 700 K and nights far below freezing
records.coreQuestion: If you lived on Mercury, how long would a day last, and how hot would it get?
records.misconception: Mercury's day isn't shorter than its year; one sunrise to the next lasts two Mercury years.
editorialTitles: The Planet Where a Day Lasts Two Years
Why Mercury Is Both Scorching and Freezing

facts.claim: One solar day (sunrise to sunrise) on Mercury lasts for around 176 Earth days, or twice Mercury's sidereal year.
Mercury's sidereal year (88.0 Earth days) and sidereal day (58.65 Earth days) are in a 3:2 ratio, in a spin–orbit resonance.
At perihelion, the equatorial subsolar point climbs to a temperature of about 700 K.
On the dark side of the planet, temperatures average 110 K (−163 °C).
The floors of deep craters at the poles are never exposed to direct sunlight, and temperatures there remain below 102 K.

narration.text: Why one Mercury day lasts 176 Earth days.
That's twice as long as its 88-day year.
It spins slowly, locked in a 3:2 dance with its orbit.
At noon, the surface can reach about 700 kelvin.
The night side averages −163 °C.
Polar craters never see sunlight at all.
With no atmosphere, nothing evens the heat out.
So the closest planet to the Sun still has frozen corners.

records.topic: What If a Comet Slammed Into Jupiter?
records.hook: Why a comet hit Jupiter at 60 km/s.
records.openingLine: Why a comet hit Jupiter at 60 km/s.
records.secondBeat: In 1994, Shoemaker–Levy 9 struck as a string of fragments.
records.scientificMechanism: Jupiter's gravity tears apart and captures passing comets, then its escape velocity sets impact speed
records.expectedConsequence: a string of fireballs leaving scars larger than Earth, visible from our telescopes
records.coreQuestion: If a comet slammed into Jupiter, what would we see from Earth?
records.misconception: Jupiter doesn't just attract impacts that would hit Earth; it also tears comets apart first.
editorialTitles: The Week a Comet Hit Jupiter
What Shoemaker–Levy 9 Taught Us

facts.claim: The comet was later observed as a series of fragments ranging up to 2 km (1.2 mi) in diameter.
These fragments collided with Jupiter's southern hemisphere between July 16 and 22, 1994 at a speed of approximately 60 km/s (37 mi/s) or 216,000 km/h.
Calculations showed that its unusual fragmented form was due to a previous closer approach to Jupiter in July 1992.
The plume from the fireball quickly reached a height of over 3,000 km (1,900 mi) and was observed by the HST.

narration.text: Why a comet hit Jupiter at 60 km/s.
In 1994, Shoemaker–Levy 9 struck as a string of fragments.
Jupiter's gravity had torn it apart in 1992.
Some pieces were up to 2 kilometres wide.
One fireball plume rose over 3,000 kilometres.
The impacts ran from July 16 to 22.
Each hit left dark scars visible from Earth.
So Jupiter works as a shredder, not just a shield.

records.topic: What If Earth Were Tilted Like Uranus?
records.hook: Why Uranus's poles get 42 years of sunlight.
records.openingLine: Why Uranus's poles get 42 years of sunlight.
records.secondBeat: Then they get 42 years of darkness.
records.scientificMechanism: a planet's axial tilt sets how sunlight shifts between hemispheres over its orbit
records.scenarioChange: Earth's axis tipped to lie nearly on its side
records.expectedConsequence: decades-long polar days and nights, and extreme seasons everywhere
records.coreQuestion: If Earth were tilted like Uranus, what would seasons be like?
records.misconception: Uranus isn't upright; it rolls around the Sun almost on its side.
visualScenes: Uranus on its side with rings
orbit showing pole facing the Sun
editorialTitles: The Planet With 42-Year Days
What If Earth Rolled Around the Sun

facts.claim: It has a marked axial tilt of 82.23°, with a retrograde rotation period of 17 hours and 14 minutes.
In an 84-Earth-year orbital period around the Sun, its poles get around 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of continuous darkness.
The planet's atmosphere has the lowest minimum temperature (49 K (−224 °C)) of all of the Solar System's planets.
As of 2026, it has been visited only once when in 1986 the Voyager 2 probe flew by the planet.

narration.text: Why Uranus's poles get 42 years of sunlight.
Then they get 42 years of darkness.
Its axis is tilted 82.23 degrees, nearly on its side.
One orbit takes 84 Earth years.
Tilt Earth like that, and each pole gets decades-long days.
Seasons would swing between endless glare and endless night.
Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus, in 1986.
So Earth's gentle seasons come from a modest tilt.

records.topic: What If a Volcano Poisoned a Country?
records.hook: Why one eruption killed 80% of Iceland's sheep.
records.openingLine: Why one eruption killed 80% of Iceland's sheep.
records.secondBeat: Laki released about 8 million tons of fluorine.
records.scientificMechanism: a long fissure eruption releases huge volumes of fluorine and sulfur gases that contaminate grass and air
records.scenarioChange: a months-long fissure eruption struck a farming nation
records.expectedConsequence: livestock die from fluorine poisoning, followed by famine
records.coreQuestion: If a volcano poisoned a country's air and grass, what would kill people: the lava or the famine?
records.misconception: Laki's deadliest effect wasn't lava; it was poisoned grazing and famine.
editorialTitles: The Eruption That Starved Iceland
Why Laki Killed With Gas, Not Lava

facts.claim: The system erupted violently over an eight-month period between June 1783 and February 1784 from the Laki fissure and the adjoining volcano Grímsvötn.
About 80% of sheep (190,500 head), 50% of cattle (11,500 head), and 50% of horses (28,000 head) died because of dental and skeletal fluorosis from the 8 million tons of fluorine that were released.
An estimated 20% of the population died in the famine after the fissure eruptions ensued, with about 8,000 excess deaths.
The gases were carried by the convective eruption column to altitudes around 15 km (50,000 ft).

narration.text: Why one eruption killed 80% of Iceland's sheep.
Laki released about 8 million tons of fluorine.
It erupted for eight months, from June 1783.
Fluorine poisoned the grass that livestock ate.
Half of all cattle and horses died too.
Famine followed, killing about 20% of the population.
Its gases rose about 15 kilometres high.
So a volcano's deadliest weapon can be invisible.

records.topic: What If the Ozone Hole Never Closed?
records.hook: Why Antarctic ozone fell 40 to 50 percent.
records.openingLine: Why Antarctic ozone fell 40 to 50 percent.
records.secondBeat: Chlorine from CFCs was tearing ozone apart.
records.scientificMechanism: chlorine from CFCs destroys stratospheric ozone, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet light
records.expectedConsequence: a growing ozone hole and far more ultraviolet reaching the surface
records.coreQuestion: If the ozone hole never closed, what would sunlight do to us?
records.misconception: The ozone hole isn't fixed forever; banning CFCs is letting it recover.
editorialTitles: What If We Hadn't Fixed the Ozone Hole
The Treaty That Saved the Ozone Layer

facts.claim: These concerns led to the adoption of the Montreal Protocol in 1987, which bans the production of CFCs, halons, and other ozone-depleting chemicals.
Recovery was projected to continue over the next century, with the ozone hole expected to reach pre-1980 levels by around 2075.
In 2019, NASA reported that the ozone hole was the smallest ever since it was first discovered in 1982.
As of 2010, Antarctic total column ozone in September and October continued to be 40–50 percent lower than pre-ozone-hole values.

narration.text: Why Antarctic ozone fell 40 to 50 percent.
Chlorine from CFCs was tearing ozone apart.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet light before it reaches us.
In 1987, the Montreal Protocol banned CFC production.
By 2019, the hole was the smallest since it was found.
Full recovery is expected around 2075.
Without the ban, far more UV would reach the ground.
So one treaty quietly changed the sky above us.

records.topic: What If the Great Dying Happened Again?
records.hook: Why 81% of marine species vanished at once.
records.openingLine: Why 81% of marine species vanished at once.
records.secondBeat: It happened about 251.9 million years ago.
records.scientificMechanism: massive carbon release disrupted climate and ocean chemistry, driving extinction over tens of thousands of years
records.scenarioChange: an extinction on the scale of the end-Permian struck today
records.expectedConsequence: most marine species and most land vertebrates lost
records.coreQuestion: If the Great Dying happened again, what would survive?
records.misconception: Mass extinctions aren't instant; the worst one unfolded over tens of thousands of years.
editorialTitles: The Worst Extinction in Earth's History
What the Great Dying Tells Us About Today

facts.claim: It is Earth's most severe known extinction event, with the extinction of 57% of biological families, 62% of genera, 81% of marine species, and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species.
The extinction occurred between 251.941 ± 0.037 and 251.880 ± 0.031 million years ago, a duration of 60 ± 48 thousand years.
The negative carbon isotope excursion lasted for approximately 500,000 years.
The decline of animal life is concentrated over approximately 10,000 to 60,000 years, with plants taking an additional several hundred thousand years to show the full impact.

narration.text: Why 81% of marine species vanished at once.
It happened about 251.9 million years ago.
70% of land vertebrate species died too.
The main extinction took about 60,000 years.
Carbon chemistry stayed disturbed for about 500,000 years.
Recovery took far longer than the collapse.
Life survived, but in a very different form.
So the worst extinction was slow, and still catastrophic.

records.topic: What If a Liquid Could Climb Walls?
records.hook: Why helium below 2.17 kelvin climbs out of cups.
records.openingLine: Why helium below 2.17 kelvin climbs out of cups.
records.secondBeat: It becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity.
records.scientificMechanism: below 2.17 K, helium-4 becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity that can flow up and over container walls
records.scenarioChange: a liquid flowed with no friction at all
records.expectedConsequence: it creeps over container rims and flows through tiny pores
records.coreQuestion: If a liquid could climb walls, what would stop it?
records.misconception: Superfluids aren't just very runny; their superfluid part has zero viscosity.
visualScenes: superfluid helium creeping over a cup rim
editorialTitles: The Liquid That Climbs Out of Its Cup
What Happens to Helium Below 2.17 K

facts.claim: This condensation occurs in liquid helium-4 at a far higher temperature (2.17 K) than it does in helium-3.
The superfluid component has zero viscosity and zero entropy.
Superfluid helium can flow relatively easily up the wall of containers, over the top, and down to the same level as the surface of the liquid inside the container.
The Infrared Astronomical Satellite IRAS, launched in January 1983, was cooled by 73 kilograms of superfluid helium, maintaining a temperature of 1.6 K (−271.55 °C).

narration.text: Why helium below 2.17 kelvin climbs out of cups.
It becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity.
It creeps up the wall, over the top, and down.
It stops only when levels inside and out match.
It can even spray upward in a fountain effect.
In 1983, 73 kilograms of it cooled a space telescope.
No ordinary seal could hold it in.
So near absolute zero, quantum rules become visible.

records.topic: What If You Could Touch Earth's Core?
records.hook: Why Earth's core matches the Sun's surface heat.
records.openingLine: Why Earth's core matches the Sun's surface heat.
records.scientificMechanism: enormous pressure keeps the iron inner core solid despite temperatures like the Sun's surface
records.expectedConsequence: a solid iron ball as hot as the Sun's surface, crushed solid by pressure
records.coreQuestion: If you could touch Earth's core, how hot would it be, and why is it solid?
records.misconception: Earth's inner core isn't molten; pressure keeps it solid even at about 5,700 K.
visualScenes: Earth cutaway to the inner core
temperature comparison with the Sun's surface
inner core size versus the Moon
editorialTitles: Why Earth's Core Is as Hot as the Sun
The Solid Ball of Fire Beneath Your Feet

facts.claim: It is primarily a solid ball with a radius of about 1,230 km (760 mi), which is about 20% of Earth's radius or 70% of the Moon's radius.
The temperature at its surface is estimated to be approximately 5,700 K (5,430 °C; 9,800 °F), about the temperature at the surface of the Sun.
In 1952, Francis Birch published a detailed analysis of the available data and concluded that the inner core was probably crystalline iron.
In 2005, shear waves were detected passing through the inner core; these claims were initially controversial, but are now gaining acceptance.

narration.text: Why Earth's core matches the Sun's surface heat.
Its surface is about 5,700 kelvin.
Yet the inner core is a solid iron ball.
Crushing pressure keeps the metal from melting.
Its radius is about 1,230 kilometres, 70% of the Moon's.
In 2005, shear waves were detected passing through it.
Touching it is impossible; no material survives the trip.
So pressure, not heat alone, decides whether rock is solid.

records.hook: Why your microbes carry 100 times your genes.
records.openingLine: Why your microbes carry 100 times your genes.
records.secondBeat: About 2 million bacterial genes, against 20,000 human ones.
records.scientificMechanism: trillions of microbes in and on the body digest food, train immunity and crowd out pathogens
records.expectedConsequence: digestion and immune defence weaken, and harmful microbes can take over
records.coreQuestion: If your microbes disappeared, what would stop working?
records.misconception: Most microbes in your body aren't enemies; many do jobs your own genes can't.
editorialTitles: What Your Body's Microbes Actually Do
Why You're Outnumbered by Microbial Genes

facts.claim: The number of bacterial genes is estimated to be 2 million, 100 times the number of approximately 20,000 human genes.
The researchers calculated that more than 10,000 microbial species occupy the human ecosystem.
Fecal microbiota transplant is approximately 85–90% effective in people with CDI for whom antibiotics have not worked or in whom the disease recurs following antibiotics.
Only about 50% of humans have easily detectable populations of methanogens.

narration.text: Why your microbes carry 100 times your genes.
About 2 million bacterial genes, against 20,000 human ones.
More than 10,000 microbial species live in and on us.
They digest food and help train your immune system.
Without them, harmful microbes could move in.
Restoring gut microbes cures 85 to 90% of some stubborn infections.
So your body works as a partnership, not a solo act.

records.topic: What If You Remembered Every Day of Your Life?
records.hook: Why fewer than 100 people remember every day.
records.openingLine: Why fewer than 100 people remember every day.
records.scientificMechanism: highly superior autobiographical memory lets a few people recall specific days in detail
records.scenarioChange: a person remembered every day of their life
records.expectedConsequence: vivid recall of dates and events, but not a perfect memory for everything
records.coreQuestion: If you remembered every day of your life, would it be a gift or a burden?
records.misconception: Hyperthymesia isn't photographic memory for everything; it's for personal life events.
editorialTitles: The People Who Remember Every Day
What Hyperthymesia Is Really Like

facts.claim: It is extraordinarily rare, with fewer than 100 people in the world having been diagnosed with the condition as of 2021.
Participants are challenged to match dates to 60 famous events that happened between the time they were five years old and the present day.
Answers must be chosen within 11 seconds to qualify for consideration.
In the aftermath of the 2006 Neurocase publication alone, more than 200 people contacted McGaugh; however, only a handful were determined to be actual cases.

narration.text: Why fewer than 100 people remember every day.
The condition is called hyperthymesia.
Testers match dates to 60 famous events.
Each answer must come within 11 seconds.
After a 2006 study, over 200 people claimed it.
Only a handful turned out to be genuine.
It covers personal life events, not everything they read.
So forgetting may be as useful as remembering.

records.topic: What If We Beamed Solar Power From Space?
records.hook: Why orbit gets 144% of Earth's best sunlight.
records.openingLine: Why orbit gets 144% of Earth's best sunlight.
records.secondBeat: In space, there's no night, clouds or air.
records.scientificMechanism: orbital solar panels collect sunlight without night or weather and beam energy to ground receivers
records.scenarioChange: large solar power stations operated in orbit
records.expectedConsequence: steady clean power, limited by launch cost and beaming efficiency
records.coreQuestion: If we beamed solar power from space, what would stand in the way?
records.misconception: Space solar power isn't blocked by physics; launch cost is the barrier.
visualScenes: microwave beam to a ground antenna
editorialTitles: Can We Beam Solar Power From Space?
Why Space Solar Waits on Launch Costs

facts.claim: The intensity in orbit is approximately 144% of the maximum attainable intensity on Earth's surface.
Caltech's MAPLE project successfully demonstrated beaming power to earth in 2023.
MAPLE transmitted an effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) of 3.2 watts, far below the kilowatts typical of commercial communications satellites.
Launch costs in the range of $100–$200 per kilogram of payload from low Earth orbit to Geosynchronous orbit are needed if SPS is to be economically viable.
In December 2019, Xinhua reported that China plans to launch a 200-tonne SBSP station capable of generating megawatts of electricity to Earth by 2035.

narration.text: Why orbit gets 144% of Earth's best sunlight.
In space, there's no night, clouds or air.
In 2023, Caltech's MAPLE beamed power down to Earth.
It sent just 3.2 watts, a proof of concept.
Viable plants need launch costs of $100 to $200 per kilogram.
China has talked of a 200-tonne station by 2035.
So space solar power is waiting on rockets, not sunlight.

records.topic: What If Your Brain Had a Chip?
records.hook: Why one brain implant carries up to 3,072 electrodes.
records.openingLine: Why one brain implant carries up to 3,072 electrodes.
records.secondBeat: Each tiny wire holds 32 of them.
records.scientificMechanism: implanted electrode threads record neuron activity so software can decode intended movements
records.expectedConsequence: people with paralysis controlling devices by thought, with surgical and long-term risks
records.coreQuestion: If your brain had a chip, what could it actually do today?
records.misconception: Brain implants don't read thoughts; they decode signals linked to intended movement.
visualScenes: thin electrode threads in brain tissue
editorialTitles: What Brain Implants Can Really Do
Inside the Race to Wire the Brain

facts.claim: Each probe contains 48 or 96 wires, each of which contains 32 independent electrodes, making a system of up to 3,072 electrodes per formation.
In April 2021, Neuralink demonstrated a monkey playing the game Pong using a Neuralink implant.
On January 29, 2024, Musk announced that Neuralink had successfully implanted a Neuralink device in a human and that the patient was recovering.
In August and September 2025, Toronto's University Health Network performed Canada's first Neuralink brain implant surgeries on two patients with cervical spinal cord injuries.

narration.text: Why one brain implant carries up to 3,072 electrodes.
Each tiny wire holds 32 of them.
They record neurons firing as you intend to move.
In 2021, a monkey played Pong with one.
In 2024, the first human received the implant.
By 2025, patients with spinal injuries were getting them in Canada.
It decodes movement signals, not private thoughts.
So brain chips restore control long before they read minds.

records.topic: What If a Particle Beam Passed Through Your Head?
records.hook: Why one man survived 2,000 sieverts to the head.
records.openingLine: Why one man survived 2,000 sieverts to the head.
records.secondBeat: In 1978, a proton beam passed through his skull.
records.scientificMechanism: a narrow high-energy proton beam deposits an enormous dose along a thin path through tissue
records.scenarioChange: a scientist's head crossed an accelerator beam
records.expectedConsequence: severe local damage along the beam path, yet survival
records.coreQuestion: If a particle beam passed through your head, could you survive?
records.misconception: An enormous radiation dose isn't always fatal when it's confined to a thin beam path.
editorialTitles: The Man Who Put His Head in a Particle Beam
How Anatoli Bugorski Survived

facts.claim: He is known for having survived a radiation accident in 1978, when a high-energy proton beam from a particle accelerator passed through his head.
Bugorski was leaning over the equipment when he stuck his head in the path of the 76 GeV (12.2 nJ) proton beam.
The exposed parts of his head received a local dose of 200,000 to 300,000 roentgens (2,000 to 3,000 sieverts).
On 3 June 1978, he was checking a malfunctioning piece of equipment when the safety mechanisms failed.

narration.text: Why one man survived 2,000 sieverts to the head.
In 1978, a proton beam passed through his skull.
Anatoli Bugorski was checking faulty equipment.
The safety mechanisms had failed.
The beam carried 76 GeV protons.
The dose along its path was 2,000 to 3,000 sieverts.
Because it was so narrow, most of his body was spared.
So where radiation lands matters as much as how much.

records.topic: What If a Star Were Flung Out of the Galaxy?
records.hook: Why one star flees at 1,755 km/s.
records.openingLine: Why one star flees at 1,755 km/s.
records.secondBeat: That's almost 0.6% of the speed of light.
records.scientificMechanism: a binary star passing close to a supermassive black hole can be split, with one star ejected at extreme speed
records.scenarioChange: a star was hurled out of the Milky Way
records.expectedConsequence: it leaves the galaxy forever at a small fraction of light speed
records.coreQuestion: If a black hole flung a star out of the galaxy, how fast would it go?
records.misconception: Black holes don't only swallow stars; they can also launch them.
editorialTitles: The Star Kicked Out of the Milky Way
How a Black Hole Launches a Star

facts.claim: S5-HVS1 is an A-type main-sequence star notable as the fastest one detected as of November 2019, traveling with a peculiar velocity of 1,755 km/s, almost 0.6% of the speed of light.
The star is in the Grus (or Crane) constellation in the southern sky, and about 29,000 light-years from Earth.
S5-HVS1 was ejected from the Milky Way galaxy after interacting with Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy.
It is possible that it was originally part of a binary system that was tidally disrupted by the supermassive black hole, causing it to be ejected.

narration.text: Why one star flees at 1,755 km/s.
That's almost 0.6% of the speed of light.
S5-HVS1 was flung out by our galaxy's central black hole.
It may have been half of a binary pair.
One star was captured, and its partner was launched.
It's now about 29,000 light-years from Earth.
It will never return to the Milky Way.
So black holes don't just swallow stars. They throw them.

records.topic: What If Earth Sat in the Great Void?
records.hook: Why one region holds 60 galaxies instead of 2,000.
records.openingLine: Why one region holds 60 galaxies instead of 2,000.
records.secondBeat: It's the Boötes void, found in 1981.
records.scientificMechanism: cosmic voids are vast regions with far fewer galaxies than average
records.scenarioChange: the Milky Way sat inside the Boötes void
records.expectedConsequence: a night sky nearly empty of other galaxies
records.coreQuestion: If Earth sat in the Great Void, what would the night sky look like?
records.misconception: The universe isn't evenly filled with galaxies; huge regions are nearly empty.
visualScenes: map of galaxies with a huge empty region
editorialTitles: The Great Nothing in Space
What If We Lived in the Boötes Void

facts.claim: It contains just 60 galaxies, which is significantly fewer than the approximately 2,000 galaxies expected for an area of comparable size.
With a radius of 62 megaparsecs (nearly 200 million light-years), it is one of the largest known voids in the visible universe.
It was discovered in 1981 by astronomer Robert Kirshner as part of a survey of galactic redshift.
Its center is located 700 million light-years from Earth.

narration.text: Why one region holds 60 galaxies instead of 2,000.
It's the Boötes void, found in 1981.
Its radius is nearly 200 million light-years.
Its center sits 700 million light-years away.
From inside, the night sky would hold almost no other galaxies.
Astronomers might not have discovered other galaxies until much later.
Galaxies gather along filaments, leaving vast gaps between.
So the universe is less a cloud than a web with holes.

records.hook: Why 0.1% of the ocean shelters 25% of species.
records.openingLine: Why 0.1% of the ocean shelters 25% of species.
records.secondBeat: It's coral reef, about half the area of France.
records.scientificMechanism: reef-building corals create complex habitat that shelters a large share of marine life
records.scenarioChange: the world's coral reefs died off
records.expectedConsequence: a quarter of marine species lose their home, along with fisheries and coastal protection
records.coreQuestion: If coral reefs disappeared, how much of ocean life would go with them?
records.misconception: Reefs aren't a big share of the ocean; their outsized role comes from habitat, not area.
visualScenes: ocean area versus species share chart
editorialTitles: What Losing Coral Reefs Would Cost
The 0.1% of the Ocean That Holds a Quarter of Its Life

facts.claim: They occupy less than 0.1% of the world's ocean area, about half the area of France.
They provide a home for at least 25% of all marine species, including fish, mollusks, worms, crustaceans, echinoderms, sponges, tunicates and other cnidarians.
Shallow tropical coral reefs have declined by 50% since 1950, partly because they are sensitive to water conditions.
The Indo-Pacific region accounts for 91.9% of this total.

narration.text: Why 0.1% of the ocean shelters 25% of species.
It's coral reef, about half the area of France.
Corals build the structure that shelters fish and invertebrates.
Shallow tropical reefs have declined 50% since 1950.
Most reefs, 91.9%, lie in the Indo-Pacific.
Lose them, and a quarter of marine species lose their home.
So the ocean's richest life depends on its smallest builders.

records.hook: Why 700 million people catch mosquito-borne illness yearly.
records.openingLine: Why 700 million people catch mosquito-borne illness yearly.
records.secondBeat: Those infections kill over one million people a year.
records.scientificMechanism: a few mosquito species transmit diseases like malaria, while most species play minor ecological roles
records.expectedConsequence: a huge drop in disease deaths, with limited but real ecological gaps
records.coreQuestion: If mosquitoes went extinct, what would we gain and what would we lose?
records.misconception: Most of the 3,600 mosquito species don't spread human disease.
editorialTitles: What If Mosquitoes Went Extinct
The Deadliest Animal on Earth

facts.claim: Mosquitoes, the Culicidae, are a family of small flies consisting of 3,600 species.
Nearly 700 million people acquire a mosquito-borne illness each year, resulting in over one million deaths.
Paleoculicis minutus is known from Canadian amber, which dates to around 79 million years ago.
Kyanne Reidenbach and colleagues analysed mosquito phylogenetics in 2009, using both nuclear DNA and morphology of 26 species.

narration.text: Why 700 million people catch mosquito-borne illness yearly.
Those infections kill over one million people a year.
Yet there are about 3,600 mosquito species.
Only a small share of them spread human disease.
Mosquitoes have existed for at least 79 million years.
Some fish and birds eat them, but few depend on them alone.
So targeting the deadly few matters more than wiping out all.
